section_summary: This section documents Japanese propaganda and suspected intelligence activity across Latin America in early 1942. Initial diplomatic reporting from Ecuador, Cuba, Guatemala, Nicaragua, and Uruguay found little overt propaganda, while more detailed reports from Peru, Argentina, and Colombia described Japanese, German, and Italian collaboration, radio and press campaigns, misleading wire-service reports, and the circulation of wartime publications. Later FBI, Army, and Navy intelligence reports allege Japanese plans to recruit airline and maritime agents, preserve clandestine communications after diplomatic ruptures, influence Latin American governments, and conduct espionage through personnel operating in Brazil, Argentina, Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, and Mexico.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 22 on Japanese propaganda and nationals in Ecuador
subfiles.about: Reports the known forms of Japanese propaganda in Ecuador and recommends tighter confinement of Japanese nationals.
subfiles.summary: The Legation had detected only a whispering campaign and propaganda pamphlets since U.S. entry into the war, and suggested asking Argentina and Chile to prevent such pamphlets from being printed. It warned that former Japanese geologists had cultivated support in Esmeraldas and that Japanese nationals nominally concentrated in Riobamba could move freely and engage in propaganda, recommending their transfer to a U.S. concentration camp.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3235 on Japanese propaganda in Cuba
subfiles.from: Ellis O. Briggs, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: States that no Japanese propaganda was then known to be circulating in Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Briggs replies to the Department’s circular inquiry concerning current Japanese propaganda. He reports that neither the Embassy nor the Chinese Minister, who closely monitored Japanese activity in Cuba, had found evidence of current dissemination.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Havana propaganda report to U.S. intelligence agencies
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards the confidential Havana despatch on Japanese propaganda for intelligence use.
subfiles.summary: The Department distributes a copy of confidential despatch no. 3235 from the American Embassy at Havana. The listed recipients are the Army’s Military Intelligence Division, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the FBI.

subfiles.title: Guatemala telegram clarifying press treatment of Japanese news
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Guatemala (Fay Allen Des Portes)
subfiles.about: Clarifies that major foreign wire services carried news about Japan but were not accused of knowingly handling Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The Legation corrects a possible misunderstanding arising from its preceding telegram. United Press, Associated Press, and Reuters were identified only as the sources of virtually all printed news about Japan reaching Guatemala, not as deliberate distributors of Japanese propaganda.

subfiles.title: Nicaragua telegram on Axis sympathizers and enemy aliens
subfiles.from: U.S. Legation, Nicaragua (Pierre de Lagarde Boal)
subfiles.about: Reports no known Japanese propaganda but warns that German, Italian, or other Axis sympathizers might conduct it.
subfiles.summary: The Legation had no evidence of current propaganda by the very small Japanese community in Nicaragua. Boal suggested that Sumner Welles emphasize to the Nicaraguan delegation at the Rio conference the need for firm measures concerning enemy aliens and their property.

subfiles.title: Montevideo telegram on Japanese propaganda in Uruguay
subfiles.about: Reports that a broad survey found no deliberate Japanese propaganda in Uruguay.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy responds to the Department’s circular inquiry. An exhaustive survey had found no Japanese propaganda deliberately disseminated through the press, radio, or other channels.

subfiles.title: Non-American Activities distribution sheet
subfiles.about: Routes material on non-American activities to numerous officers for suggestions and return.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists officers in several Department of State units who could review attached material. A brief handwritten comment appears at the bottom but is largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2591 with Elejalde letter and press clippings
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Warns that U.S. news reports and magazine commentary could lend credibility to Axis and Japanese propaganda in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Norweb transmits a letter from César Elejalde Chopitea arguing that American news material written for domestic readers could be damaging when translated and circulated in Latin America. Elejalde criticizes a George T. Hughes article on Japan’s difficult economic position as effectively justifying Japanese aggression, and condemns Time’s treatment of Bolivia, Ecuador, and Chile. The enclosed El Comercio article describes Japan’s economic dependence and wartime shortages, while La Noche calls for banning Time over alleged insults to South American nations.

subfiles.title: Fragment of a Lima despatch on anonymous propaganda mailings
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Discusses anonymous Japanese and German-style propaganda mailed in Peru and possible forensic comparison of the envelopes.
subfiles.summary: The page continues a discussion of a Japanese news bulletin and a circular urging Peruvian neutrality at the Rio conference. Norweb believed the Japanese Legation or Central Japanese Society may have distributed the bulletin and suspected German authorship of the circular. He enclosed envelopes for comparison with known German Legation typewriter samples.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3922, Japanese Propaganda in Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Surveys the organization, personnel, media, themes, and effectiveness of Japanese propaganda in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Japanese propaganda intensified from June 1941 and was coordinated across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Mexico, later operating alongside Nazi, Fascist, and Falangist networks. It identifies Albino Pugnalin, Antonio J. de Silva Souza, and George Yoshio Shinya as prominent figures and describes newspapers, magazines, radio, cultural lectures, tourist literature, and newsreels as principal outlets. Although Japanese military news could impress some Argentines, the report concludes that racial attitudes and unfamiliar Japanese ideological themes limited the campaign’s effectiveness.

subfiles.title: Department of State summary, Japanese Propaganda in Argentina
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the principal findings of despatch no. 3922 concerning Japanese propaganda in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum condenses the Embassy’s description of coordinated cultural societies, radio propaganda, periodicals, tourist and commercial literature, lectures, newsreels, and cooperation among Domei, Transocean, and Stefani. It reiterates the roles attributed to Pugnalin, de Silva Souza, and Shinya and concludes that initial Japanese military successes had more influence than Japanese propaganda itself.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting wartime publications to the Library of Congress
subfiles.about: Sends publications received from U.S. posts in Buenos Aires and Agua Prieta for the Library’s wartime collection.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary continues the Department’s practice of forwarding wartime material distributed in the other American republics. The enclosed publications accompanied despatch no. 3922 from Buenos Aires and despatch no. 22 from the consulate at Agua Prieta, Sonora.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report no. 25 fragment on German agents, advisers, and raiders in East Asia
subfiles.about: Reports alleged German-Japanese intelligence collaboration, German technical advisers in Japan, political influence, procurement, and plans for commerce raiding.
subfiles.summary: The fragment begins with reports of Chinese-agent recruitment for operations in Thailand, Burma, and Malaya, followed by a detailed listing of German technical personnel at Japanese naval, aviation, industrial, and chemical-warfare sites. It alleges that the German ambassador sought to unify Japanese pro-Axis forces and encourage action against the Soviet Far East. Additional sections concern acquisition of strategic raw materials in Siam and alleged plans to arm German ships in Japan for attacks on U.S. shipping to Vladivostok.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Japanese Tokyo Club Syndicate
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file containing a report on the Japanese Tokyo Club Syndicate and its affiliations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a cross-reference for a Navy Department report on the activities of the Japanese Tokyo Club Syndicate and its interlocking affiliates. The original was filed under decimal number 894.20211/517.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office routing sheet
subfiles.from: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office, Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides an internal routing form for liaison and records handling.
subfiles.summary: The page consists almost entirely of departmental unit abbreviations and routing spaces. A receipt stamp dated January 19, 1942, indicates its administrative use.

subfiles.title: Military intelligence report on Japanese travelers observed by Dean Kyle
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department (Levi G. Brown)
subfiles.about: Records Dean Kyle’s observations of Japanese travelers in Latin America and George Comnas’s encounter with a boastful Japanese passenger.
subfiles.summary: Dean Kyle reported little visible German or Italian propaganda but noticed numerous Japanese travelers moving purposefully and being met by groups at railway stations. George Comnas of Standard Oil described a Japanese passenger traveling toward Caracas who displayed many maps, predicted that Japan would defeat the United States, and carried a large quantity of silver pesos. The incident had reportedly been communicated to the U.S. Embassy in Caracas.

subfiles.title: Dreier note on United Press and Havas despatches in Colombia
subfiles.about: Calls attention to a report on United Press and Havas stories published in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Dreier advises McDermott that the attached report on wire-service despatches in Colombia may be of interest. He also notes that Mr. Toop of the Division of the American Republics wants the report returned.

subfiles.title: Non-American Activities distribution sheet for the Colombia report
subfiles.about: Circulates material on non-American activities for review and return to Mr. Toop.
subfiles.summary: The form contains a long list of officers eligible to review the material. It directs that the papers be returned to Mr. Toop after suggestions are made.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3552 with Colombian press clippings on harmful United Press and Havas reports
subfiles.about: Documents Japanese and Axis claims circulated in Colombian newspapers under United Press and Havas datelines.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy argues that purportedly reputable United Press and Havas reports gave Japanese propaganda undeserved credibility in Colombia. It cites claims about Singapore, Wake Island, Pearl Harbor, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, and Japan’s alleged peaceful intentions toward South America, and suggests approaching the wire services or their correspondents. The many enclosed Spanish-language clippings reproduce Japanese and Axis accounts of military victories, Allied losses, Japanese strategic plans, and the supposed weakness or imminent defeat of Allied positions.

subfiles.title: Index-and-return slip
subfiles.about: Requests prompt indexing and return of the accompanying material.
subfiles.summary: The printed slip asks that the material be indexed and returned within a checked interval. A February 13, 1942, stamp appears on the page, but the selected turnaround instruction is unclear.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Un Japonés y un Suramericano
subfiles.from: Rodolfo O. Rivera, American Library Association
subfiles.about: Sends a publication as evidence of Japanese activity in South America.
subfiles.summary: Rivera tells Thomson that a copy of Un Japonés y un Suramericano by Remy Rurema and Teikichi Okinura is being sent under separate cover. He characterizes it as material for the Department’s collection of evidence concerning Japanese efforts in South America.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on a German Gestapo center in Japan
subfiles.about: References allegations that Germany was creating a Gestapo center in Japan for operations in South America.
subfiles.summary: The note points to a Justice Department letter alleging that Germans intended to operate in South America from a Gestapo center in Japan. It also mentions an enclosed letter from Dr. Kindermann outlining cultural-relations plans between Japan and South America.

subfiles.title: Hoover letter transmitting intelligence on Japanese plans for Latin America
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a highly confidential FBI memorandum on Japanese activities and plans in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards intelligence obtained from confidential sources and requests highly confidential treatment. He notes that the same information was also being supplied to the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs and the Coordinator of Information.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities and Plans for Latin America
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary Adolf A. Berle Jr. and designated interagency recipients
subfiles.about: Outlines alleged Japanese intelligence, propaganda, bribery, clandestine communication, and Axis-cooperation plans throughout Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum alleges plans to collect U.S. information through travelers, Pan American Airways employees and facilities, airline passengers, and maritime contacts, while concentrating propaganda in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile. It describes themes designed to discredit the United States, preserve Latin American neutrality, exploit Catholic and Iberian connections, cooperate with German and Italian agents, bribe Chilean officials, and use Havas correspondents for communications. Country sections allege clandestine addresses and Spanish diplomatic assistance in Peru, intelligence and radio monitoring in Brazil, and Domei arrangements with Argentine news services and covert addresses in Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Instruction no. 2051 transmitting the FBI memorandum to Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Sends the February 26 memorandum on Japanese activities and plans for Latin America to the Embassy in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary forwards the confidential intelligence memorandum for the Buenos Aires Embassy’s information. The instruction notes that copies were also being sent to the embassies at Lima and Rio de Janeiro.

subfiles.title: Instruction no. 1071 transmitting the FBI memorandum to Lima
subfiles.about: Sends the February 26 memorandum on Japanese activities and plans for Latin America to the Embassy in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary forwards the confidential intelligence memorandum for the Lima Embassy’s information. Copies were also being transmitted to the embassies in Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Instruction no. 2402 transmitting the FBI memorandum to Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Sends the February 26 memorandum on Japanese activities and plans for Latin America to the Embassy in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary forwards the confidential intelligence memorandum for the Rio de Janeiro Embassy’s information. It states that copies were also being sent to Lima and Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office routing form
subfiles.from: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office, Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides a blank internal distribution and records-routing form.
subfiles.summary: The page lists Department of State offices and abbreviations without substantive narrative. It appears to be an administrative cover sheet associated with incoming intelligence material.

subfiles.title: Naval intelligence report on Ignacio Bonife
subfiles.about: Reports pro-Japanese remarks made in Valparaíso by a Filipino crewman aboard the Santa Lucia.
subfiles.summary: Ignacio Bonife, a Filipino messman on the Grace liner Santa Lucia, reportedly became drunk during a stop at Valparaíso and praised Japan. He claimed that the Philippines would benefit under a “Greater Asia,” and the information was passed to Grace Lines authorities.

subfiles.title: ONI report on suspected Japanese spies and mercury smuggling in Mexico
subfiles.about: Identifies suspected Japanese intelligence officers and links their movements to agent placement and a concealed mercury shipment in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The report names Eitaro Yoshioka, Rinkai Kaneko, Tadakumi Waki, and Atunori Utida as dangerous Japanese spies believed to be placing agents aboard Pan American aircraft and ships serving South America. It also describes the status of Japanese diplomatic and military personnel in Mexico, Bolivia, Peru, and Bogotá, including alleged plans directed toward the Panama Canal. A final section recounts an October 1941 attempt at Manzanillo to export contraband mercury concealed in drums billed as bronze and suggests that the Japanese officers may have been involved.
